You're on a submarine carrying a nuclear torpedo, and the Americans are bombing you. Your captain wants to fire it. Only you can stop him.
It's October 1962, the Cuban Missile Crisis. Your submarine is hiding near Cuba, and you haven't heard from Moscow in days.
The batteries are dying. The air conditioning is dead. It's over forty-five degrees inside, and sailors are fainting at their posts.
Then American warships find you, and start dropping depth charges all around the hull.
Your captain thinks the war has already started. He orders the nuclear torpedo made ready.
We will die, he shouts, but we will sink them all.
But on this submarine, firing it needs three officers to agree. The captain says yes. The political officer says yes.
You argue, and you calm him down. Finally, the submarine rises to the surface, surrounded by American ships.
Back home, nobody calls you a hero. One officer says it would have been better if you'd gone down with your ship.
Your story stays secret for forty years. You die in 1998, before the world ever hears it.
Then in 2002, it finally comes out. And one American historian says it plainly. A guy called Vasili Arkhipov saved the world.
